## Authors' Response to Round 1

Response to Reviewers
Morgan et al. “Mechanistic snapshots of lipid-linked sugar transfer
We are thankful for the overall positive and constructive feedback from the Reviewers. Here we
provide a point-by-point response to their comments:
Reviewer #1:
The manuscript by Morgan et al. describes the use of time-resolved cryo-EM (cryo-TREM) on
the bacterial transmembrane glycosyltransferase GtrB. The objective is to attempt to identify
conformational states during the catalysis of undecaprenol phosphate (UndP) glucosylation to
obtain UndP-Glc. The study is very well performed and the manuscript well written. There are
however major issues in the interpretation of the experimental cryo-EM maps that seriously
challenge the proposed mechanism.
We thank the Reviewer for their assessment of our study. While we respectfully disagree with
the Reviewer’s conclusions regarding our cryo-EM maps, we have taken their comments as
constructive criticism, and have addressed each point in detail below. We have also included
additional validations to support our data, and also note that our MD simulations and kinetic
assays provide further independent support for the experimental results.
1) Choice of methodology
The cryo-TREM method is not new but still under development. The strength of the technique is
that it can capture conformational changes of dynamic proteins that may be dificult to obtain
with conventional cryo-EM or X-ray crystallography. However, cryo-TREM works best for
proteins that undergo large conformational changes and is of more limited use for proteins like
GtrB where the catalytic cycle is driven by a series of subtle structural changes within a confined
region of the protein.
We respectfully disagree with that cryo-TREM is not broadly applicable to enzymatic reactions.
While to date cryo-TREM has indeed primarily been demonstrated on proteins undergoing large
conformational changes (ref. 10, ref. 11, and ref. 12), our UV-based approach presented here is
designed to address this limitation. Our method enables the capture of faster millisecond
dynamics, particularly of enzymes, aiming to observe tightly controlled mechanisms, a gap that
has remained unresolved in the field. We describe more below on how this was key to
understanding the mechanism of GtrB catalysis.
The drawback of using the method on GtrB is apparent from inspecting the cryo-EM density for
the proposed states which all show similar overall structural arrangement in the donor, metal
and acceptor binding sites, but with varying degree of disorder (convolution of states and
flexibility) in the fine details that are of actual biological interest such as side chain and loop
conformations, metal coordination etc. The structural states presented for GtrB can be captured
with conventional high-resolution techniques (X-ray and cryo-EM) and give experimental maps
with better definition and less disorder, as has already been done previously for several GT2
glycosyltransferases (soluble and membrane integrated).
While traditional cryo-EM and X-ray crystallography may achieve higher resolutions, we believe
it is not accurate to characterize our approach as unsuccessful. Our reconstructions reached 2.6–
2.8 Å for a membrane protein with inherent flexibility. Although the conformational changes in
GtrB were less extensive than initially anticipated, we resolved a highly coordinated mechanism
supported by both MD and SMD simulations. Moreover, the generation of the product-bound
state demonstrates that a complete catalytic cycle was captured, rather than an artifact of
“varying degrees of disorder.” We argue that the structural states captured in this study,
especially those like the pre-catalysis state, are not easily capturable by conventional techniques.
Capturing the donor-acceptor complex as we did for the substrate-bound state represents in our
opinion a rarity. This is underrepresented in the literature (see ref. 18) as the sugar-donor is
usually present as an empty nucleotide, thus requiring the use of our caged-substate approach.
While the authors have done an excellent effort trying to apply cryo-TREM on GtrB, the current
study does not provide substantial new understanding of this class of glycosyltransferases
beyond previously reported structures of GtrB and other GT2 glycosyltransferases. One new
result of the present study is the re-tracing of the density of the loop connecting the two
transmembrane helices TM1 and TM2. TM1 and TM2 were incorrectly connected in the previous
study from 2016. While this correction is important, it does not provide the level of scientific
novelty expected for this journal and would likely be more appropriate for a journal with a
different focus.
We disagree with the assessment that the information gained from our investigation is not
substantial. Our work introduces a time-resolved cryo-EM approach that, to our knowledge, has
not previously been applied to membrane-bound glycosyltransferases. Using a caged substrate,
we were able to capture GtrB in substrate-bound, pre-catalysis, and product-bound states within
milliseconds of reaction initiation, providing direct visualization of catalytic events that were
previously inaccessible.
These structures uncover mechanistic details not previously described, including the
coordination of UndP by key arginine and lysine residues, the role of a swinging tryptophan
residue in product release, and the dynamic reorganization of the lipid substrate during catalysis.
Our combined use of structural variability analysis, MD simulations, and kinetic assays further
validates the proposed reaction mechanism and the order of catalytic events. Importantly, our
observations suggest a reassignment of potential catalytic residues (D94/Q98), providing
mechanistic insight that challenges prior assumptions about D157 as the catalytic acid.
Finally, our results have implications beyond bacterial GtrB, offering insight into the dynamic
mechanisms of related eukaryotic enzymes such as Dolichol Phosphate Mannose Synthase
(DPMS) and advancing the broader field of lipid-linked glycosyltransferases. Taken together, our
study provides both methodological innovation and substantive mechanistic understanding of
glycosyltransferase catalysis.
2) Analysis of the catalytically relevant states 9NYC, 9NYD, 9NYK
9NYC: The map is stated by the authors to correspond to the substrate-bound state with bound
donor substrate UDP-Glc and acceptor substrate UndP. The density for the Glc moiety in UDP-
Glc is very weak in all four subunits. The density of UndP is also ambiguous, especially with
respect to the connection to the phosphate group. Since the map is obviously convoluted by
several conformers, the state cannot be unambiguously assigned as the substrate-bound state of
GtrB, and interpretation of details belonging to that state (metal binding, side chain
conformations, ligand binding etc) is therefore not possible.
In our model 9NYC, the map was refined with C4 symmetry, and each chain contains the same
substrate-bound state. The density for UndP is robust to model up to the third isoprene unit and
the position of the phosphate head is consistent with our previous tungstate-replacement X-ray
crystallography results (ref. 20). The head position is also in agreement with the DolP-bound
model of PfDPMS (ref. 21). The phosphate head is positioned in the conserved R122/R125
pocket with a local resolution from 2.5-3 Å, similar to the surrounding area. Included are three
videos showing the density of the map for both UndP and UDP-Glc (Response to Reviewers
Videos 1-3). Additionally, our unbiased MD simulations further validate the stability of the UndP
in this state across all four chains (Extended Data Figure 9e; formally 7e), and of the protein
backbone (shown below). A more detailed explanation of the stability of each state validated by
our MD is included in our response to Reviewer #3.
The Glc moiety density is indeed weaker than that of UndP, but it is sufficient to model and
position relative to UndP, having a local resolution closer to 3 Å. We note that Glc is not strongly
coordinated within the active site, leading to considerable rotational freedom, which could result
in poorer density. The inherent rotational freedom is supported by our unbiased MD data as well
as our kinetic assays, which suggested promiscuity in the active site with similar binding strength
of UDP-Gal, UDP, Glc, and caged-UDP-Glc when compared to UDP-Glc (see Figure 4d). We
have added a description of these details in the text (lines 174-179). This is also consistent with
the Glc moiety needing to undergo a conformational change during the reaction (i.e. transfer onto
UndP) meaning its position is transient and dynamic.
The substrate-bound state was separated independently from the product-bound and pre-catalysis
states and does not share particle sets with those reconstructions. In addition, the particles
underwent three rounds of 3D classification, yielding a largely uniform set. While it is possible
that several thousand particles represent alternative states, the final reconstruction is based on
>500,000 particles, strongly enriching for the most dominant conformer, as we consider typical
in cryo-EM studies. However, we do not claim that this state corresponds to time = 0 or
immediate post-substrate-binding, and we are in total agreement with the Reviewer that such an
assignment would be premature. However, guided by MD and steered MD simulations, as well
as comparisons with PfDPMS (ref. 21) and ArnC (ref. 22 and ref. 23) structures, we place this
conformation earlier than the pre-catalysis and product-bound states. Thus, while we remain
cautious about its exact temporal placement, the dominance of this conformer in the dataset
suggests it represents a stable and functionally relevant state. Given this, we believe that based
on the quality of the density, interpreting features such as metal binding, side-chain
conformations, and ligand interactions are both justified and informative. We added this
explanation to lines 188-191 of the manuscript.
9NYD: The map is stated by the authors to correspond to a mixture of pre-catalysis and product-
bound states. Specifically, subunits A/B/D are supposed to contain the substrates UDP-Glc and
UndP, and subunit C would contain the products UDP and UndP-Glc. The region containing the
donor and acceptor-binding sites (including the loop delineating his region) is heavily
disordered and convoluted. The binding of substrates and/or products cannot be confirmed, and
modeling of the loop is also not trustworthy due to extremely low definition of the backbone (and
even worse for the side chains).
We thank the Reviewer for this comment and agree that the density in the membrane-facing loop
(specifically β7-JM2) in subunits B/C/D of model 9NYD is difficult to interpret for both the
backbone and sidechains. Subunit A contains sufficient density to completely model the β7-JM2
loop consistent with the substrate-bound state. Thus, we have decided not to include residues
201-206 in the product-bound state or subunit C (residues 200-206 were removed in the pre-
catalysis state or subunit B, and in subunit D) because the modeling was based on the substrate-
bound state and not on the density. This change does not alter the conclusions of our study,
however we agreed with the Reviewer that the modeling of the loop was not justifiable, and have
corrected this accordingly (lines 206-208 and lines 215-217).
We believe that in subunit B (the pre-catalysis state) there is clear and interpretable density for
UndP and the Glc moiety at our recommended contour level (0.142). Included are videos
showing the density of the map for both UndP and UDP-Glc (Response to Reviewers Videos 4-
6). Both steered and unbiased MD simulations confirmed the stability of this state; in unbiased
MD, the structure remained stable without reverting to the substrate-bound state, while in steered
MD, we were able to sample the pre-catalysis state with minimal applied force, yielding a near-
identical conformation to the experimental cryo-EM map. Furthermore, recent preprint data on
the related ArnC enzyme demonstrated a so-called ‘State 3’ in MD simulations (ref. 23, see
Figure 6A) that closely parallels our experimentally observed pre-catalysis state.
In subunit C (product-bound state), we believe the density for the product UDP and UndP-Glc is
of sufficient quality to model, with a local resolution between 2.5 and 3Å. Included are videos
showing the density of the map for both UndP-Glc and UDP (Response to Reviewers Videos 7-
9). Our product-bound state closely resembles the product-bound conformation of the related PP-
GT PfDPMS bound to DolP-Man (ref. 21, see Figure 3b). Finally, MD simulations confirmed the
stability of this product-bound state across four replicates, which we have included in an updated
Extended Data Figure 10h (formally Extended Data Figure 8) and an acknowledgement in the
text (lines 267-268). Our steered MD simulations recapitulated the product release pathway,
including the conformational change of W207 (demonstrated in Supplemental Video 5),
consistent with our cryo-EM observations.
9NYK: The map is stated by the authors to correspond to a pre-intermediate state. Specifically,
UDP-Glc and UndP has been modeled in all four subunits. The map has serious disorder. If
contouring the map at a very low level (close to noise level) there is some possible residual
density for a Glc moiety bound to UDP but no density for UndP in any of the subunits. This state
is probably a disordered donor-bound state.
We acknowledge the Reviewer’s comment, but our results suggest that at our recommended
contour level (0.149), density for the Glc moiety is present in all four subunits, and density is
observed for at least the partial isoprenyl tail of UndP in each case. That said, this model is not
central to our main conclusions and was included only to illustrate the lowering of the β7–JM2
loop observed in other models. The positioning of UndP above UDP-Glc does not appear to play
a significant role in the catalytic mechanism and in our opinion may instead reflect diffusion of
the substrate within the active site. To avoid overinterpretation, we have elected to remove this
model from the study rather than assign it as a donor-bound state, which we do not believe would
necessarily be completely accurate. Thus, we have revised Extended Data Figure 2 and 6 without
the pre-intermediate state and removed its mention in the text. The PDB model (9NYK) and map
(EMD-49935) will still be available for those that are interested.
3) Correction of GtrB topology
p.6. The improved density for the TM1-TM2 loop allowed correction of the topology of TMD.
The disordered density for this loop in the previous GtrB structures led to the incorrect tracing of
TM1-TM2 connection such that TM1 in one subunit was connected to TM2 in a nearby subunit.
Since the reassignment of the TMD is an important result of the present study, this should be
more clearly described in the text and in Ext.Data 2D. As it is presented now, it is difficult for
even an experienced structural biologist to get a clear understanding of the original error in
models 5EKE/5EKP.
We agree with the Reviewer that this particular section could be confusing for those not familiar
with the original study. A revised Extended Data Figure 2d has been amended with better clarity
for the updated TM assignment and additional explanation has been added to the text (lines 120-
124).
Reviewer #2:
This manuscript by Morgan and co-workers delivers several snapshots of GtrB during the
glycosyltransferase reaction catalysed by this enzyme. The aim is rather challenging, since GtrB
is a membrane protein, and the authors design a time resolved cryoEM experiment using a caged
photolabile UDP-Glc derivative. This substrate is activated by UV light just prior to grid
freezing so the reaction is observed within 50-70 ms. Buy analysing one cryoEM sample of
working GtrB, the authors separate several states by 3D classification and postulate a
mechanism of action. Their model is supported by MD simulations.
The topic is sound, since lipid glycosylation is a universal process required to construct
glycosylated cellular membranes. The manuscript is clear and well written, and the figures are
really good.
We thank the Reviewer for their kind comments and assessment of our study.
I just have one overall concern. Although the figures of rendered maps seem to support the
separation of some catalytic states, I have some doubts about the classification strategy.
It seems that the catalytic events can be understood in the context of one subunit (as depicted in
Figure 5b) with no need for large or concerted conformational changes between subunits. The
refinement and the classification (Extended Data Figure 4) have been performed at the level of
the tetramer, even after symmetry expansion. With no information about the relative catalytic
states of monomers within a tetramer, it is reasonable to expect mixtures of subunits within the
tetramers after classification. Actually, two of the conformations (product-bound and pre-
catalytic states) are seen in different subunits within the same tetramer).
The only way to circumvent this potentially large heterogeneity would be to work subunit-wise at
the level of refinement and classification. Thus, a D4 symmetry expansion (instead of D1) and a
classification within a mask covering one subunit (instead of a full tetramer) could deliver more
clear separation of uniform states. Maybe the authors tried this, or the authors can give a good
reason not to use this strategy.
The Reviewer raises an important point regarding the use of D1 versus D4 symmetry when
analyzing variability among GtrB particles and are grateful for this. We agree that D4 symmetry
expansion can, in principle, provide insight into monomer-specific movements rather than
tetramer-wide variations. We tested this approach by taking 3DVA-selected particles, expanding
to D4, and performing 3D classification with a tight mask around a singular monomer. While the
apparent resolution was artificially improved, likely due to oversampling, the resulting maps
were substantially noisier, less ordered, and lacked distinct variability. This likely reflects the
very large number of D4 symmetry-expanded particles (>6 million) used in classification.
For this reason, we chose to use D1 symmetry expansion, which reduced the dataset size
(~700,000 particles) and produced maps with greater clarity, while still capturing the tetramer-
wide variations of interest. Moreover, although GtrB functions catalytically as a monomer, it is
physiologically a tetramer, and we felt it was important to preserve this context in the maps. We
have added additional explanation to this reasoning in the text (lines 164-166).
Additionally, GtrB tetramers associate in double tetramers. The authors do not discuss at any point
whether this association can have any sort of impact in the functioning of the enzyme. One
possibility could be to perform some of the MD simulations using the double tetramer instead of
the tetramer.
We agree with the Reviewer that this requires an explanation. In our previous study (ref. 20),
GtrB also formed a head-to-head dimer of tetramers in the crystal lattice, suggesting this is a
stable state adopted by the purified enzyme in both detergent and lipid nanodiscs. This
arrangement reflects an in vitro interaction between two residues on stacking tetramers (Q58 and
R61) and cannot form under physiological membrane conditions, where GtrB functions as a
single membrane-embedded tetramer. Nevertheless, the enzyme remains catalytically competent
in the octameric state. This is evidenced in our previous study (ref. 20) in which kinetic assays on
crude, solubilized membranes and assays in proteoliposomes both yielded consistent results. We
also add that the formation of the product, as evidenced by our product-bound state in the cryo-
EM data, further leads us to believe that the enzyme remains functional in the octamer state. In
our view, this indicates that each monomer can catalyze the reaction independently (as opposed
to an allosteric modulation model). We have added an explanation of this in the text (lines 306-
310).
Because the octameric assembly may not be stable within a single bilayer, our MD simulations
focused on the physiologically relevant tetrameric form, thereby linking the cryo-EM structure to
the native state of the enzyme. Performing molecular dynamics simulations of the octamer would
require a double-membrane system and non-physiological conditions. Such a setup would
involve non-standard practices (e.g., atomic fluctuations are drastically reduced), making any
apparent “stability” in MD an unreliable indicator of true thermodynamic stability. We have
decided not to pursue this avenue.
Reviewer #3:
In this study, the authors successfully resolved multiple conformational states of GtrB (substrate-
bound, pre-catalysis, product-bound and pre-intermediate states), using cryogenic time-resolved
electron microscopy (cryo-TREM) combined with UV photolysis of a caged substrate. It shows
insights into the catalytic mechanism of GtrB. The integration of structural data, MD simulation
data and biochemical assays provides a framework for understanding glycosyltransferase
mechanisms.
We thank the Reviewer for their comments and overall assessment of our study.
However, there are still some key issues that need to be addressed in this study, a major revision
is necessary.
1. In the authors’ previous study (reference 4), the authors proposed the catalytic mechanism of
GtrB, no catalytic base is needed, D157 was suggested as a catalytic residue. However, in this
study, the authors suggested that D94 or D157 could be the catalytic base, so further
experimental validation (mutagenesis with kinetic assays) is still needed to resolve this
ambiguity.
We agree with the Reviewer that this remains an ambiguous point. To address it, we originally
performed mutagenesis of D94 and D157 and attempted to incorporate these variants into
liposomes, as we did with other mutants in this study. D157N successfully incorporated into
liposomes, but as with all other tested mutants exhibited a diminished ability to efficiently bind
UDP-Glc when compared to wild-type. We contend that mutation at these sites effectively
renders the enzyme catalytically “dead.” Although the D94 and D99 mutants were successfully
expressed, repeated attempts to reconstitute them into liposomes for uptake assays were
unsuccessful (Extended Data Figure 12a, formally Extended Data Figure 9a). In our original
study (ref. 20), a D157N mutant abolished activity, consistent with the interpretation that D157
may function as the catalytic base. Nevertheless, this assignment remains debated in the field,
and mutagenesis alone may not provide a definitive answer, as such substitutions can disrupt
folding or metal coordination, or simply the electrostatics of the active site in a way that
jeopardizes function. In our discussion, we suggest that D94 could be the more likely candidate,
as related enzymes such as ArnC (ref. 23) point towards a mechanism by which the DxD motif
engages in catalysis rather than strictly metal coordination. Our cryo-EM data, however, show an
equidistant UndP position to both D94 and D157. The evidence from our previous study, which
shows that mutation at D157 abolishes activity in crude membranes and incorporated liposomes,
is further supported by the kinetic assays in the present study.
2. In most glycosyltransferases, there is a conserved DXD motif, of which the two ASP residues
are coordinated with Mn2+ or Mg2+. And there is also a third residue (most likely HIS residue)
coordinated with Mn2+ or Mg2+. Even though the authors provided suggestions of the DXD
(D94, D96), possibly Q98 could be the third coordinated residue, no structure obtained in this
study showed a complete coordination around Mg2+. Why is that? This is a critical question.
Previous mutagenesis studies suggest that mutations of the two ASP or the third residues could
greatly reduce the enzymatic activities. If the DXD motif and the third residues could not
coordinate with Mg2+ stably, how could the catalysis happen? At least, the authors need to
address this question.
While the deposited PDB files may appear to lack complete Mg²⁺ coordination, this largely
reflects the limitations of PDB deposition rules, which impose strict criteria on assigning metal
coordination bonds. To avoid over-interpretation, we took a conservative approach and did not
assign bonds that were not automatically assigned during deposition. So, while we originally had
modelled complete coordination of the Mg2+ in nearly all of the presented states, which is
supported by the density, we defer to the PDB deposition to stay consistent with other entries. We
note that in the deposited pre-catalysis state there remains complete coordination of the Mg2+.
Importantly, in membrane-bound glycosyltransferases with a DxD motif, only one aspartate is
observed to coordinate the Mg²⁺ ion at a time. Across all known acceptor PP-GT enzymes, the
first aspartate of the motif (D89 in PfDPMS (ref. 21), D94 in GtrB, and D100 in ArnC (ref. 22
and ref. 23) does not participate in Mg²⁺ coordination, making it a plausible candidate for
catalytic function.
Based on our observations, we propose that Q98 may instead contribute to the motif, effectively
replacing D94’s classical role. We consistently observe Q98 coordinating the metal in several
states, and in 9NYD chain B (the pre-catalysis state) we observe complete Mg²⁺ coordination
(between the two phosphates groups of UDP, Q98, and D96). While we remain cautious in
assigning a definitive catalytic residue, these structural and comparative data support Q98 as a
strong candidate for metal coordination.
3. The authors stated that multiple conformational states of GtrB were captured experimentally,
substrate-bound, pre-catalysis, product-bound and pre-intermediate states. The authors used the
distance between the phosphate group of UndP and C1 of the glucose of the donor as a criterion
to describe the substrate-bound, pre-catalysis and pre-intermediate states. 2500-ns MD
simulations were performed for the three systems, respectively. The authors should also include
the distance plots showing the dynamics of the three conformational states. Are all three
conformational states stable?
To assess the stability of the experimentally captured states, we analyzed both the key
intermolecular distances and the Root Mean Square Deviation (RMSD) of the backbone of the
protein and of the ligands throughout the MD simulations. Our analysis confirms that all three
states—substrate-bound, pre-catalysis, and product-bound—are dynamically stable. In the
following figures, we report both the graph obtained with simulations performed with TIP3P
and with OPC solvent models, as suggested in a following comment by the Reviewer.
In the substrate-bound state, our simulations revealed significant flexibility of the glucose moiety
on UDP-Glc. This is expected, as this part of the substrate is solvent-exposed and lacks strong,
stabilizing interactions with the protein. This flexibility naturally leads to fluctuations in the
distance between the UndP phosphate headgroup and the C1 atom of glucose in the substrate-
bound state.
However, the UndP itself remains stably anchored in its binding pocket. The RMSD plot for the
UndP phosphate and its first two isoprene units shows low deviation, confirming that this part of
the substrate maintains the conformation observed in the cryo-EM structure, considering the
fluctuations at room temperature.
For the pre-catalysis state, the distance plot between the UndP headgroup and the glucose C1
atom is particularly informative. The distance is consistently maintained between 4 and 6 Å,
which is close to the distance found in our cryo-EM structure. The observed fluctuations around
this value are expected, as our MD simulations at ambient temperature capture the system's
thermal energy, unlike the static, low-temperature cryo-EM experiment.
Finally, in the product-bound state, the UndP-Glc product also remains globally stable. The
RMSD plots show slightly higher values compared to the substrate-bound UndP, which can again
be attributed to the flexibility of the newly transferred glucose moiety.
In addition to these analyses, the distance plots in the original Extended Data Figures 7-8 (now
Extended Data Figures 9-10) and in the new Extended Data Figures 7 and 8 show the stability of
the interactions of UndP with the surrounding residues in the different states.
In summary, despite the expected thermal fluctuations and the flexibility of the sugar groups, all
three states remain in their distinct conformations throughout the simulations and do not
spontaneously transition into one another, thus confirming the stability of the states captured
experimentally.
4. In this study, the authors claimed that the catalytic mechanism of GtrB is elucidated. In their
previous study (reference 4), the authors proposed one. However, further investigation is still
needed to fully elucidate the catalytic mechanism. A QM/MM study is highly recommended in the
near future.
We thank the Reviewer for their suggestion, which we will keep in mind for future studies.
Some other comments:
1. References are not recommended to be cited in the Abstract.
We thank for Reviewer for catching this.
2. A table listing the conformational states for each chain of the structures is recommended
An updated Extended Data Table 2 has been amended with relevant chain numbers.
3. For the MD simulations, the authors used Amber ff19SB force field for protein and TIP3P
water model. In the FF19SB paper (J. Chem. Theory Comput. 2020, 16, 528−552), the authors
clearly recommend against using FF19SB with TIP3P water model, but with OPC water model.
How do the authors comment on this issue?
We thank the Reviewer for raising this important point regarding the choice of the water model.
The selection of a water model in a multi-component system, such as our membrane-protein-
ligand complex, often involves balancing the optimal parameter sets for each component. While
we are aware that the OPC water model is recommended for Amber ff19SB, the combination
with TIP3P remains a robust and published approach. For instance, a recent, extensive
benchmark study (J. Chem. Inf. Model. 2021, 61, 284–297) on protein-ligand binding
thermodynamics explicitly used the Amber ff19SB force field in combination with TIP3P water
for all their simulations, demonstrating the validity of this setup in the recent peer-reviewed
literature. Furthermore, it is important to note that the ff19SB parameter set is specific to the
protein, whereas our ligands and membrane lipids were modeled with GAFF2 and Lipid21,
respectively—force fields that are well-established for use with TIP3P. Our choice, therefore,
represented a balanced approach for this complex system.
Nevertheless, to rigorously ensure that our conclusions are robust and not dependent on this
choice, we have taken the reviewer's suggestion as an opportunity to perform a cross-validation.
We conducted a new set of simulations for all systems using the recommended OPC water model
(3 replicates of 1μs for each system). We now include a two new Extended Figures (Extended
Data Figure 7 and 8) that provides a direct comparison of key geometric parameters (including
ligand RMSD and the specific distances discussed in the main text) between the original
simulations with TIP3P and the new ones with OPC. The plots demonstrate near congruence
between the results obtained with both water models, confirming the stability of the observed
conformational states in both setups.
This agreement validates the robustness of our original findings and strongly indicates that our
conclusions are independent of the specific water model used. We thank the Reviewer again, as
their insightful comment has allowed us to add a further layer of validation to our study.
4. In the MD simulations, how did the authors choose the force field parameters of Mg2+? It was
not mentioned in the Methods sections. Furthermore, the authors also assigned two bonds
between the Mg2+ and two phosphate oxygen atoms, respectively, while still keeping the net
charge of -2e for Mg2+. Have the authors verified the parameters? Is it reasonable?
The accurate parameterization of divalent cations like Mg²⁺, particularly their coordination
geometry, is a well-known challenge for classical force fields. As no predefined parameters exist
for the specific coordination environment in our system, we initially employed a standard non-
bonded model (the amber Mg2+ ion parameter), relying on the default electrostatic and van der
Waals interactions. While this model was stable in most simulations, we observed in a subset of
our long-timescale simulations (>500 ns) a gradual loss of the native coordination geometry. We
believe this instability is a known artifact arising from small inaccuracies in the non-bonded
force field, which can sometimes fail to fully capture the quantum mechanical nature of metal
coordination over extended timescales, rather than a physically meaningful event.
To prevent this artifact and ensure the structural integrity of the catalytic site throughout the
simulation, we introduced weak harmonic distance restraints between the Mg²⁺ ion and the
coordinating oxygen atoms. The equilibrium distance for these restraints was set to the precise
value observed in our experimental cryo-EM structure. This strategy offers two key advantages:
- It anchors the simulation to high-quality experimental data, ensuring the catalytic site
maintains a physically realistic geometry.
- The restraints are ‘soft’, meaning they allow for natural thermal fluctuations around the
equilibrium distance but prevent the larger, unphysical dissociation events seen with the
pure non-bonded model.
Regarding the ion's parameters, the Mg²⁺ was always treated as a non-bonded particle with a
formal charge of +2e. The restraints are an additional potential energy term and do not represent
covalent bonds; they do not alter the ion's charge or its electrostatic interactions. A hybrid
approach similar to this was already proposed for simulating other metalloenzymes, as it corrects
for known force field limitations while preserving the system's dynamics. Please, see for
example the following works:
1. Hu, L., & Ryde, U. J. Chem. Theory Comput. 2011, 7, 2452–2463.
2. Shen, R., et al. PLOS Comput. Biol. 2015, 11, e1004368.
3. Foster, C. A., & West, A. H. (2017). Proteins: Structure, Function, and Bioinformatics,
85, 155-176.
We have now clarified this procedure in the SMD Methods section in the revised manuscript.
5. In the steered MD simulations, the authors applied positional restraints on the Mg ions, what
is the purpose of this?
The purpose of applying positional restraints to the Mg²⁺ ion was to ensure that the steering force
acted specifically on the translocating lipid, preventing an artificial destabilization of the
catalytic site. For the UndP entrance simulations, our collective variable (CV) was defined as the
distance between the UndP headgroup and the Mg²⁺ ion itself. Without restraints, the external
force applied along this CV would be directly exerted on the ion. As we observed in preliminary
tests, this caused the Mg²⁺ to be pulled from its coordinating residues, leading to an unphysical
collapse of the catalytic site's geometry. The restraints were therefore essential to study the lipid's
movement while keeping the enzyme's core machinery intact.
For the product exit simulations, a different CV was used where the Mg²⁺ ion was not the direct
reference. However, the tangential nature of the pulling force required to extract the product from
the pocket generated a rotational torque on the protein. In this case, we maintained the same
positional restraints on the Mg²⁺ ions for two reasons: first, to act as a stable anchor to cancel this
simulation-induced torque, and second, to maintain methodological consistency across both sets
of SMD simulations.
This approach ensures that in both processes, the work performed and the conformational
changes observed are representative of the lipid's translocation, providing a more physically
realistic depiction of the events.
6. In the manuscript, the authors mentioned that UndP is a 55-carbon isopreoid, however, in the
cryo-EM structure, it is not. In the MD simulations, it is 55-carbon again. The authors should
comment on it.
We have expanded our explanation in the manuscript to clarify our methodology. As correctly
noted, our cryo-EM model includes only the first five isoprenyl units of UndP. This is because
the experimental density for the remainder of the 55-carbon tail was not resolved, likely due to
its high flexibility within the membrane environment of the nanodisc. Therefore, we built into
the map only the portion of the substrate for which we had clear structural evidence. For the MD
simulations, however, it was crucial to include the full-length, 55-carbon lipid to accurately
represent the complete substrate and its interactions within a continuous lipid bilayer. To achieve
this, the unresolved portion of the tail was computationally modeled onto the experimentally
derived headgroup using Maestro (Schrödinger Suite). The initial conformation was built to
adopt a low-energy state, occupying the available space within the membrane along the z-axis.
Crucially, during the subsequent extensive equilibration phase, this modeled portion of the UndP
tail was left completely unrestrained. This allowed it to freely relax and equilibrate its
conformation within the lipid bilayer, driven by natural physical interactions with the
surrounding lipids. This ensures that the final, equilibrated structure and its dynamics are not an
artifact of the initial modeled placement but are instead representative of a physically plausible
state. This approach allows us to bridge the gap between the static, density-limited experimental
structure and a more complete, dynamic model of the enzyme–substrate complex in a realistic
membrane environment.
It is also recommended to show the interactions between UndP and the lipids during the
unbiased MD and steered MD simulations.
The simulated lipids are present in both the unbiased and steered MD simulations, but they are
hidden for clarity in the Supplementary Videos otherwise it may be difficult to observe the
movement of UndP or UndP-Glc. We have included a short video of the steered MD simulation
of the UndP-Glc exit from the active site with the lipids shown (Response to Reviewers Video
10). We also added the lipids to the attached trajectories; all skipped every 100 frames (10 ns).
7. In Figure 5a, the phosphate group of UndP is protonated, but in the MD simulations, it is not
protonated. Why is that?
In Figure 5a, the protonation of the UndP phosphate reflects our assignment of D157 as a
catalytic base, in contrast to its assignment as a catalytic acid in our previous study (ref. 4). UndP
is often depicted as doubly deprotonated in physiological pH, but this is likely an
oversimplification. At physiological pH, UndP is most likely a mixture of mono- and double-
deprotonated molecules, possibly also depending on local membrane environment and salt
concentration. If the UndP that goes into the active site is double-deprotonated, then catalysis can
happen as soon as UndP is coordinated in a catalytically permissive position. No deprotonation is
necessary. But, if a mono-deprotonated UndP enters the active site, the second proton will need
to be abstracted for catalysis to happen. Thus, a catalytic base in the vicinity will be required.
The protonation state cannot be directly determined from the cryo-EM data, and whether GtrB
uses a catalytic acid or base remains unresolved. Based on precedent from related enzymes ArnC
(ref. 22 and ref. 23) and PfDPMS (ref. 21), we chose to assign D157 as a catalytic base. MD
simulations were conducted using the double-deprotonated UndP molecules due to the ambiguity
of the possible catalytic base in GtrB, whereas the figure recognizes that for a certain portion of
UndP molecules the deprotonation will be necessary, thus the possible catalytic bases
accomplishing the deprotonation are depicted. Our MD simulations are also not intended to
simulate the complete chemical reaction as this occurs on a larger timescale; rather they aim to
validate the stability of the experimental cryo-EM models. Thus, protonation states at the time of
reaction are not as relevant as the physiological conditions that GtrB may experience during
substrate binding, UndP translocation, or product exit.
8. The recommended abbreviation of steered molecular dynamics should be SMD, not sMD.
We have made this correction in the text.
9. For the SMD, page 43 lines 952-953:
“In accordance with Jarzynski equality, we reported only the minimum path work computed over
the replicates for the two processes.”
Jarzynski equality is an ensemble average, how did the authors determine the minimum path
work?
We thank the Reviewer for this important clarification. In our study, we performed a total of 12
independent SMD simulations. We achieved this by pulling over three system replicas and four
independent steering events (one per each monomer chain). In the revised version, we report all
corresponding work profiles in a new Extended Data Figure 11. We focused our analysis just on
the trajectory with the lowest total work as a practical representative of the Jarzynski-weighted
ensemble average. Indeed, because the exponential average is dominated by the lowest-work
realizations, the trajectories with minimal total work contribute the most to the free-energy
estimate, see Response to Reviewers Figure 1 and 2, top panels.
10. page 43 lines 955-958:
“The free energy barrier is computed as half of the work computed during the simulations,
assuming that the simulated process is 2 to 5 orders of magnitude faster than the predicted
characteristic time (reference 62)”
For the SMD simulations, this only applies to fast pulling (10 m/s = 10 nm/ns or faster, check the
reference 62). In this study, the pulling is 0.005 nm/ns, far slower than the slow pulling (1 nm/1ns
= 1m/s) in the reference. So it is incorrect to apply this rule here.
The empirical “½ × Work” relation cited from ref. 62 was originally proposed for cases where
the driven process occurs “at least three orders of magnitude faster” than the corresponding
spontaneous timescale, rather than for a specific absolute pulling velocity. Indeed, the absolute
velocity should consider the intrinsic diffusivity of the system along the reaction coordinate, that
would be different for different systems. In our simulations, the a-posteriori estimation of the
transition rate, using the ½ correction, indicates that the steered process is indeed 3–5 orders of
magnitude faster than the expected spontaneous event, which in our view justifies the use of this
approximation. Moreover, the corrected values are consistent with realistic kinetic scales,
whereas omitting the correction would imply first-passage times on the order of days or months.
Notably, removing the correction only increases the implied timescale, reinforcing our main
conclusion that the event is far slower than the times accessible to unbiased MD.
Furthermore, the pulling speed is too slow, less than the dynamics in unbiased MD simulations.
Possible noise could be introduced in such a slow and long SMD simulations. Pulling a distance
of 5 angstrom, 10 ns SMD is already enough, the number of pulling can be much bigger, which
could greatly increase the accuracy of the free energy barrier. Of course, metadynamics is also
recommended.
Regarding the pulling speed, in this circumstance, we respectfully disagree with the Reviewer.
Our estimations indicate that the simulated process is at least three orders of magnitude faster
than the spontaneous one. It is important to recall that equality between the external work
performed during a perturbation and the corresponding free-energy difference is achieved only in
the reversible limit, i.e., for an infinitely slow process, as stated by the Second Law of
Thermodynamics. Other free-energy methods, such as Umbrella Sampling or Restrained MD,
reconstruct the free-energy difference from a series of quasi-equilibrium states through
thermodynamic integration.
In contrast, for far-from-equilibrium perturbations such as SMD, Jarzynski’s theory establishes
that the average work equals the true free-energy difference for any perturbation, but only if a
sufficiently large number of trajectories are available. Ref. 62 notes that when the dissipative
bias exceeds ~15 kBT, “the number of required samples becomes prohibitively large for both
simulations and experiments.” Based on this consideration, we performed SMD at the slowest
feasible pulling speed while using multiple replicas, within our available computational
resources. In our case, reducing the simulation time, as suggested by the Reviewer, would
increase dissipation rather than improve accuracy.
To directly verify this, we also tested the Reviewer’s suggestion by performing additional
simulations at 0.1 and 1 nm/ns for the substrate-bound state. None of these faster pulls yielded a
lower total work than the slower protocol (see Response to Reviewers Fig. 1), even if five times
more replicas are conducted (five independent replicas from three independent equilibrated
system).
Moreover, the mean work, the exponential average, and the standard deviation were all smaller
for the slower pulling speed, confirming that slower SMD reduces dissipation and hysteresis, as
expected. We also performed analogous fast-pulling tests for the product-bound state, at 1 nm/ns,
which also in this case resulted in substantially higher barriers (Response to Reviewers Fig. 2).
In this case, the fast pulling prevents proper molecular rearrangement of the loop and the
surrounding cavity, leading only to high-energy paths. The new fast-pulling SMD simulations
were conducted using another water model, OPC, as a comparison to show that the water model
does not affect significantly the processes; see also the comment above.
Overall, thanks to the Reviewer’s suggestion, we could confirm that among all simulated
trajectories, the one reported in the original version of the main manuscript most likely
represents the physically correct and energetically consistent path.
We also emphasize that our goal was not to compute a complete free-energy profile, but rather to
identify and characterize plausible transition pathways connecting the relevant states.
11. The authors shared the MD data, however, for each of the systems, only a number of
snapshots were selected to share. Different systems have different number of snapshots (hundreds
to thousands), which make the simulation data less authentic.
We thank the Reviewer for noticing this. We adjusted all the files extracting the reduced
trajectories using the same timestep, 10 ns.
